what_it_does: When designing a computer chip, the very last physical layout step — called 'legalization' — takes cells that a placement tool has roughly positioned and snaps them to legal grid locations without overlapping each other. In a 3D integrated circuit (a chip stack where multiple layers of silicon are bonded together), this is harder because overflowing cells can move not only within one layer but potentially across layers, and minimizing how far cells get displaced is critical for timing. 3D-Flow models the 3D grid of chip bins as a network (graph) and borrows a technique from logistics: finding shortest-path 'augmenting routes' through the network to move excess cells to empty spots with the least total displacement, similar to how a shipping algorithm reroutes packages. A branch-and-bound step picks the best path at each decision point, and a follow-up 'cycle-canceling' pass further reduces displacement after the main routing is done.
